Pour Kassandra Kernisan, c’est son expér: For Kassandra Kernisan, her own experience pointed the way. The entrepreneur, who works to bring the benefits of wellness initiatives to marginalized groups, is now devoting herself to a cause just as close to her heart: the advancement of Black youth. She tells us how she goes about it, with a radiant smile and a quiet strength in her gaze.
<strong>Vous êtes directrice générale de: You are the executive director of DESTA Black Youth Network. What is the organization’s mission?
<strong>‍</strong><l1>DESTA</l1> est une: ‍DESTA is a charitable organization that has existed in Montréal for 15 years. It is dedicated to closing the gaps that young Black adults face in finding jobs, pursuing their education and, as a result, moving forward in society. Because of systemic racism and language barriers, it is hard for English-speaking Black youth to navigate Quebec and Montréal society.
Nous les aidons essentiellement à surmon: Essentially, we help them overcome these systemic barriers through a range of training, employability and entrepreneurship programs.
‍<strong>LC : On entend peu parler de la: ‍LC: We rarely hear about the reality of Black anglophones here. How do you experience that?
<strong>‍</strong>C’est vraiment importa: ‍It’s really important to me to be able to help young people overcome what I had to overcome myself. My brothers and I grew up in New Jersey, to Haitian parents. We lived in the United States before moving to Luxembourg, and then I came to Montréal to study when I was 17. That’s when I discovered Montréal. My experience at McGill University was somewhat traumatic at the time, 20 years ago. I was often the only Black person in my classes. I felt isolated, I felt like I didn’t belong, or like I couldn’t connect with the others.
De plus, je n’avais pas pu naviguer plei: On top of that, I hadn’t been able to fully navigate university life, for lack of money, resources and support. My experience at McGill left me with a limited view of Montréal, geographically and socially speaking. After I finished my studies, I realized I was truly at a disadvantage as a Black, English-speaking woman. It was a shock; it wasn’t what I had envisioned. I felt like I was left with very little, even though I had a degree.
La réalité est que beaucoup d’étudiants: The reality is that many international students leave Montréal after their studies.
Je faisais partie de ceux qui voulaient: I was one of those who wanted to stay in the city and build a career here. It was extremely hard for me. Even with some basic knowledge, the language was a huge thing to overcome. It didn’t come naturally to me. I immersed myself in francophone environments, I took French classes.
Quelques années plus tard, je suis retou: A few years later, I went back to school to do an MBA in a bilingual program at HEC.
‍<strong>À la lumière de votre travail e: ‍In light of your work and your experience, what obstacles do young Black anglophones face?
Personne n’aime reconnaître qu’il a des: Nobody likes to admit they have racial biases. If you look at the system, at how it was built in North America, you end up realizing it’s a system built on racist ideologies. Closer to home, if you look at the history of Black anglophones in Montréal, you can see that they were really confined to certain careers.
Beaucoup vivaient dans le quartier de la: Many lived in the Little Burgundy neighbourhood because they were porters or worked in the railway sector. It was one of the only jobs available to an English-speaking Black person in Montréal. A few generations later, it’s an obstacle whose traces we can still see. The statistics clearly show that for a Black anglophone, the employment rate is half that of any other demographic group, and that’s for people with the same level of education.
Les Noirs anglophones n’ont pas de résea: Black anglophones don’t have strong networks, and that is especially important. When young Black people land a good job, they often find themselves in environments where they feel isolated. They can experience racial microaggressions which, over time, take a toll on someone who is already in an environment where they feel isolated, different, maybe out of place. That can lead the person to leave, to fall into depression, or worse. These are not enriching environments for our youth. And then there is, of course, language. Some say it’s easy to overcome, that it’s simply a matter of learning French. That’s partly true.
Mais il y a un fossé politique, surtout: But there is a political divide, especially when young people see what their elders went through, how they were treated as anglophones in Quebec. Even when there is a willingness to learn the language, in Quebec there is sometimes political resistance. We have to address that side of things too.
<strong>Comment faire pour corriger ce p: What can be done to fix this problem and improve the situation?
<strong>‍</strong>Il y a tellement de tr: ‍There is so much work to do, particularly at the government level. They say they stand in solidarity and want to offer support, including by injecting funds into programs that support Black communities in Canada, but there is still a denial of systemic racism. There could be greater awareness-raising, for example through campaigns on systemic racism. People really need to feel comfortable speaking up and acknowledging that we have all been conditioned to think a certain way.
Bien des entreprises sont à la recherche: Many companies are looking for talent and, lately especially, they’re looking for Black talent. That’s great. But often we run into resistance when we want to know what work they are prepared to do to make their environment more inclusive. When it comes to equity, diversity and inclusion, we see that few companies are willing to take steps to truly embrace diversity. They don’t seem to understand that diversity has positive effects on results and profitability.
Ce n’est pas comme si elles leur faisaie: It’s not as though they’re doing Black people a favour by hiring them. It’s in the company’s interest to be able to retain these employees and get the best out of them. It’s something that benefits everyone. At DESTA, we also look a lot at entrepreneurship. I think there is so much untapped talent, knowledge, skill, creativity, invention, services and ideas within our community.
Nous avons du mal à les mettre sur le ma: We struggle to bring them to market because we simply don’t have the resources and access to financing. I think that really puts us at a disadvantage. And it puts society as a whole at a disadvantage, because society doesn’t benefit from those ideas.
‍<strong>Quel message souhaitez-vous fai: ‍What message would you like to share with young people?
<strong>‍</strong>Aux jeunes qui éprouve: ‍To young people who are struggling right now, I would say: you are not alone. There are resources here for you. DESTA is one of them, but there are so many other organizations doing different things to support the Black community. There are no limits to what you can be. Often we are conditioned to think, particularly because of the education system, that we can only become certain things.
Je pense qu’il s’agit de faire ressortir: I think it’s about bringing out young people’s abilities, their natural talents, what they’re passionate about. That’s not what happens at school; they don’t get encouragement at school. It’s often the opposite. You might think there are limits, but there are always ways to get past them. Don’t be afraid to be different, celebrate your differences, because those differences are what will create change in our society.
Nous ne voulons pas que la société soit: We don’t want society to be the same in 10 or 20 years; we want it to be different, we want it to be better. So we need different people, people who feel excluded – accept yourselves, be yourselves and speak up, it’s really important.
